title: The Pigeonhole Principle
subject: Combinatorics
statement: If m objects are placed into n boxes and m > n, some box contains at least two objects. More generally, some box holds at least the ceiling of m/n objects.
short: You cannot fit more letters than pigeonholes without doubling up somewhere.
long: The principle is almost embarrassingly simple, yet it is one of the most reusable ideas in combinatorics. The general form says that averaging forces some container to hold at least the ceiling of m/n objects, even when you do not know which one. Its power lies in choosing the right 'objects' and 'boxes' — remainders, residues, birthdays, or partial sums — so that a collision becomes meaningful.
proof: If every box held at most ⌈m/n⌉ − 1 < m/n objects, the total would be less than n·(m/n) = m, contradicting that all m objects were placed. For m = n+1, the bound ⌈(n+1)/n⌉ = 2 gives the familiar two-in-one-box case.
consequence: It yields divisibility facts from remainders, guarantees birthday coincidences, and is the engine behind the Erdős–Szekeres monotone-subsequence argument.

title: The Inclusion–Exclusion Principle
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The size of a union is the alternating sum of the sizes of all intersections: add single sets, subtract pairwise overlaps, add triple overlaps, and so on.
short: Correct an overcount by removing overlaps, then undo the over-removal, repeating until nothing is left.
long: When sets overlap, summing their sizes counts shared elements more than once. Inclusion–exclusion repairs this systematically by alternating signs across every nonempty intersection. The same identity works for measures, probabilities and weighted sums, and it delivers closed formulas for derangements and surjections where direct counting is awkward.
proof: Fix an element belonging to exactly k of the sets. Its total contribution to the right side is ∑_{j=1}^k (−1)^{j+1} C(k,j) = 1 − (1−1)^k = 1, exactly what it contributes to the union; summing over elements proves the identity.
consequence: It counts derangements and surjections onto a finite set, and it computes Euler's totient function by sieving the integers not divisible by any of a set of primes.

title: The Binomial Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: In the expansion of (x + y)^n, the coefficient of x^k y^(n−k) is the binomial coefficient C(n,k).
short: Each term records a choice of which of the n factors contributes an x rather than a y.
long: Multiplying out n copies of x+y produces 2^n ordered choices, but terms with the same number of x's collect together. The number of ways to choose k of the n factors to supply an x is C(n,k), which is precisely that coefficient. Setting x = y = 1 recovers the fact that a row of Pascal's triangle sums to 2^n.
proof: In the product, choosing x from exactly k of the n factors and y from the remaining factors yields the monomial x^k y^(n−k). There are C(n,k) such choices, and like terms collect with that multiplicity.
consequence: It is the bridge between algebra and counting, gives the binomial distribution, and extends to noninteger exponents through Newton's generalised binomial series.

title: Vandermonde's Identity
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Choosing n objects from two groups at once can be split according to how many come from the first group; the resulting sum is a single binomial coefficient.
short: One committee chosen from two pools can be counted all at once or by splitting it between the pools.
long: The identity is the algebraic shadow of a counting argument: split an n-element choice from a pool of r+s objects into k taken from the first pool and n−k from the second. Terms outside the natural range for k are simply zero. Equivalently, it is the coefficient of x^n in (1+x)^r(1+x)^s = (1+x)^(r+s).
proof: Coefficient extraction gives [x^n](1+x)^(r+s) = [x^n](1+x)^r(1+x)^s = ∑_k C(r,k)C(s,n−k). Combinatorially, partition the n-subsets according to how many elements they take from the r-element part.
consequence: It is the prototype of convolution identities for binomial coefficients, underlies the hypergeometric distribution, and is the finite case of Chu–Vandermonde in hypergeometric series.

title: The Handshaking Lemma
subject: Combinatorics
statement: In any finite graph, the sum of all vertex degrees equals twice the number of edges, so the number of vertices of odd degree is even.
short: Every handshake has two hands, so the total number of handshakes counted at people is always even.
long: Counting each edge once at each endpoint gives two incidences per edge, so the degree sum is even. Since an even sum can contain only an even number of odd terms, odd-degree vertices come in pairs. Euler used exactly this observation in 1736 to show that the seven bridges of Königsberg cannot all be crossed in a single walk.
proof: Double-count the incident pairs (v, e) with v an endpoint of e: grouping by vertex gives ∑_v deg(v), while grouping by edge gives 2|E|. The parity of that even sum forces an even number of odd-degree vertices.
consequence: It decides when Euler tours can exist, shows that a regular graph of odd degree has an even number of vertices, and seeds parity arguments such as the complexity class PPA.

title: Cayley's Formula for Labelled Trees
subject: Combinatorics
statement: There are exactly n^(n−2) trees on n labelled vertices; equivalently, the complete graph on n vertices has n^(n−2) spanning trees.
short: A formula so clean it hides a bijection: labelled trees are counted by short sequences of labels.
long: For n = 4 the 16 labelled trees can be drawn by hand, but the general count n^(n−2) is startling. Prüfer gave a bijection between such trees and sequences of length n−2 drawn from the n labels, which makes the formula immediate. Variants of the same idea count spanning trees of arbitrary graphs through the matrix–tree theorem.
proof: Prüfer coding repeatedly deletes the smallest leaf and records its neighbour, producing a sequence in [n]^(n−2). The inverse attaches the smallest unused label to each recorded neighbour in turn, rebuilding the tree uniquely; a bijection gives n^(n−2) trees.
consequence: It anchors the enumeration of spanning trees, feeds random-graph connectivity thresholds, and is the simplest case of the matrix–tree theorem for weighted graphs.

title: Sperner's Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The largest family of subsets of an n-element set in which no member contains another has size C(n, floor(n/2)).
short: The widest level of the Boolean lattice — all subsets of the middle size — is the largest possible antichain.
long: An antichain forbids containment, so taking all subsets of size floor(n/2) certainly works. Sperner proved that nothing larger can: the Boolean lattice can be partitioned into symmetric chains, and each chain can contribute at most one member to an antichain. The number of chains is exactly the middle binomial coefficient.
proof: The LYM inequality ∑_{A∈F} 1/C(n,|A|) ≤ 1 follows by counting maximal chains, each of which meets F at most once. Since C(n,|A|) ≤ C(n,floor(n/2)) for every A, we obtain |F|/C(n,floor(n/2)) ≤ 1.
consequence: It is the founding result of extremal set theory, extended by the Erdős–Ko–Rado and Kruskal–Katona theorems, and supplies width bounds for antichains throughout order theory.

title: Dilworth's Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: In a finite partially ordered set, the fewest chains needed to cover every element equals the size of the largest antichain.
short: The widest row of a poset tells you exactly how many increasing chains it takes to cover it.
long: No two elements of an antichain can lie in the same chain, which gives the easy lower bound. Dilworth's achievement is the matching upper bound: a poset of width w can always be covered by w chains. The result is equivalent to several cornerstones of combinatorics, including König's theorem and Hall's marriage theorem.
proof: Encode x < y as an edge from a left copy of x to a right copy of y in a bipartite graph. A matching of size m joins comparable pairs and yields |P|−m chains, so w ≤ |P|−m. A minimum vertex cover C leaves the elements whose copies are outside C forming an antichain, so |C| ≥ |P|−w; König's theorem supplies a matching of that size and hence a cover by w chains.
consequence: It gives the minimum number of increasing subsequences covering a sequence (patience sorting), underpins Birkhoff's representation of finite distributive lattices, and complements Mirsky's dual theorem.

title: Ramsey's Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For any sizes r and s, a large enough complete graph, however its edges are coloured red and blue, must contain a red r-clique or a blue s-clique.
short: Enough structure cannot be avoided: every finite colouring of a large enough graph creates a monochromatic pattern.
long: For r = s = 3 the magic number is 6: among any six people there are three mutual acquaintances or three mutual strangers. Ramsey's theorem guarantees such a finite threshold for every pair of sizes and for any finite number of colours. The inductive bounds are enormous, and determining exact Ramsey numbers is notoriously difficult.
proof: Induct on r+s and set N = R(r−1,s)+R(r,s−1). Fix a vertex v: either it has at least R(r−1,s) red neighbours or at least R(r,s−1) blue neighbours. In the first case those neighbours contain a red (r−1)-clique or a blue s-clique; with v, either outcome gives a red r-clique or a blue s-clique.
consequence: It launched Ramsey theory — the study of unavoidable structure — and reaches into number theory, geometry, theoretical computer science and infinite combinatorics.

title: The Happy Ending Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Any five points in the plane with no three collinear contain four that form a convex quadrilateral. More generally, sufficiently many such points force n in convex position.
latex: 5\ \text{points in general position}\Longrightarrow \exists\ 4\ \text{in convex position};\qquad H(n)<\infty
short: Five well-placed points already force a convex quadrilateral — the smallest case of a broad geometric principle.
long: Erdős and Szekeres named the problem after the romance it supposedly helped spark: two of its early contributors later married. If the convex hull of five points has four or more vertices, the conclusion is immediate. Otherwise the hull is a triangle containing two of the points, and a short parity argument on the line through those two produces the quadrilateral.
proof: If the hull has at least four vertices, done. Otherwise the hull is a triangle ABC with interior points P and Q. The line PQ leaves two of A, B, C on the same side, say A and B; since P and Q lie on the same side of line AB, the four points A, B, P, Q are in convex position.
consequence: It began combinatorial geometry, leaves the exact value of the threshold H(n) open for n ≥ 7, and is closely related to the Erdős–Szekeres monotone subsequence theorem.

title: The Twelvefold Way
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Counting functions from an n-element set to a k-element set, with or without injectivity or surjectivity and up to permutations of either end, gives twelve fundamental problems.
latex: k^n,\quad k^{\underline{n}},\quad k!\,{n\brace k},\quad \binom{n+k-1}{n},\quad S(n,k),\quad p_k(n)
short: One table organises permutations, combinations, multisets, set partitions and number partitions as twelve cases of one question.
long: Rota's classification asks how many functions f from an n-set to a k-set exist once you decide whether f must be injective or surjective, and whether you identify functions that differ by permuting the domain, the codomain, or both. The answers range from k^n and falling factorials to Stirling numbers and integer partitions. A seeming zoo of formulas becomes a single three-by-four grid.
proof: Three conditions on f (any, injective, surjective) times four equivalence relations (identity, permute the domain, permute the codomain, permute both) give twelve cases. For instance, up to permuting the codomain a surjection is just a partition of the domain into k blocks, counted by the Stirling number S(n,k).
consequence: It is a compact map of elementary enumeration, reused in sampling models, in the algebra of Stirling numbers, and as the starting point for Pólya-style counting under group actions.

title: Burnside's Lemma
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number of distinct objects up to symmetry is the average, over a finite group of symmetries, of the number of objects each symmetry leaves fixed.
short: Count what each symmetry leaves unchanged, average over the group, and you get the number of genuinely different objects.
long: When a finite group acts on a set of colourings, two colourings in the same orbit represent the same object. Burnside's lemma converts the hard problem of listing orbits into the easier one of counting fixed points for each group element. It is the counting counterpart of the orbit–stabiliser theorem and is also called the Cauchy–Frobenius lemma.
proof: Count pairs (g, x) with g·x = x: summing over g gives ∑_g |Fix(g)|, while summing over x gives ∑_x |Stab(x)|. Orbit–stabiliser says |Stab(x)| = |G|/|Gx|, so that sum is |G| multiplied by the number of orbits.
consequence: It counts distinct necklaces, cube colourings and chemical isomers up to rotation, and it leads directly to Pólya's enumeration theorem via cycle indices.

title: Catalan Numbers
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The nth Catalan number counts correctly matched bracket strings with n pairs, and also triangulations of an (n+2)-gon, Dyck paths and full binary trees.
short: One sequence keeps resurfacing whenever a recursively split object is counted — a recurring surprise in combinatorics.
long: The numbers 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42 turn up in wildly different problems: matching parentheses, triangulating polygons, counting binary trees, and lattice paths that never rise above the diagonal. All share the same recursive structure — split an object at its first return to the starting state — which yields the convolution recurrence and then the closed formula. Stanley collected more than sixty such interpretations.
proof: A Dyck word of length 2n+2 decomposes uniquely as ( w₁ ) w₂, with Dyck words of sizes i and n−i, giving C_{n+1} = ∑_{i=0}^n C_i C_{n−i}. For C(x) = ∑ C_n x^n this says C = 1 + xC², whose solution with C(0) = 1 has coefficients C_n = C(2n,n)/(n+1).
consequence: It is a gateway to bijective combinatorics and generating functions, and it appears in parsing, polygon triangulations, noncrossing partitions and the associahedron.

title: The Rogers–Ramanujan Identities
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Partitions into parts congruent to 1 or 4 mod 5 are as numerous as partitions into parts differing by at least 2; a companion identity replaces these by 2, 3 mod 5 and parts at least 2.
short: Two quite different rules for building partitions produce exactly the same counts — a mod-5 miracle.
long: The first identity equates partitions whose parts are congruent to 1 or 4 modulo 5 with partitions whose successive parts differ by at least 2. The second uses residues 2 and 3 modulo 5, matched with partitions whose parts differ by at least 2 and whose smallest part is at least 2. Found by Rogers in 1894 and rediscovered by Ramanujan, they are the archetype of partition identities, with analytic, bijective and representation-theoretic proofs.
proof: Both sides are generating functions. The infinite products encode partitions with restricted residues by the q-Pochhammer symbol (a;q)_∞, while q^(n²)/(q;q)_n encodes partitions into n parts with gaps of at least 2 (and q^(n²+n)/(q;q)_n adds the condition that the smallest part is at least 2). Rogers proved the series–product equalities analytically.
consequence: They connect partition theory, basic hypergeometric series, modular forms, affine Lie algebras and vertex operator models, and they appeared in Baxter's solution of the hard-hexagon model.
